F1.quote: CoAuthor is a human-AI collaborative writing dataset that captures rich interaction between 63 writers and four instances of GPT-3 across 1445 writing sessions in English.
F1.claim: the dataset's definition of itself: a human-AI collaborative writing dataset of interactions between 63 writers and four instances of GPT-3 across 1445 writing sessions in English
F1.lineage: what it is: a human-AI collaborative writing dataset of 1445 sessions

F2.quote: At each session, we provided writers with a prompt (black text) and an instance of GPT-3.
F2.claim: at each session the makers gave a writer a prompt and an instance of GPT-3
F2.lineage: the session: prompt, writing, suggestions, editing

F3.quote: They then wrote freely (brown), asked GPT-3 for suggestions (blue), accepted the suggestions or dismissed them, and edited the accepted suggestions or previous texts in any order they chose.
F3.claim: writers wrote freely, asked GPT-3 for suggestions, accepted or dismissed them, and edited accepted suggestions or earlier text in any order
F3.lineage: the session: prompt, writing, suggestions, editing

F4.quote: All interactions between the writers and the system were recorded at the keystroke level (e.g. inserting text, moving the cursor, and receiving suggestions) with timestamps, so that we could replay them precisely.
F4.claim: every interaction was recorded at the keystroke level with timestamps, so that sessions can be replayed precisely

F5.quote: Using this rich, nuanced, and fine-grained interaction dataset, designers can examine the same sessions from multiple analytical perspectives to better understand the generative capabilities of large language models.
F5.claim: the dataset's stated purpose: designers can examine the same sessions from several analytical perspectives to understand the generative capabilities of large language models
F5.lineage: purpose: the capabilities of language models, read from interaction

F6.locus: home page, Overview: types of writing

F6.claim: creative writing: 830 stories by 58 writers; argumentative writing: 615 essays by 49 writers

F7.claim: the prompts came from the WritingPrompts subreddit and The New York Times

F8.claim: the writers were qualified crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk
F8.lineage: the writers: crowd workers, held under identifiers

F9.claim: the interface: a text editor in which pressing the tab key gives five suggestions

F18.quote: However, their highly context-dependent capabilities are difficult to grasp and are often subjectively interpreted.
F18.claim: the problem the paper states: the capabilities of language models are highly context-dependent, difficult to grasp and often subjectively interpreted
F18.lineage: the problem: capabilities context-dependent and subjectively interpreted

F19.quote: In this paper, we argue that by curating and analyzing large interaction datasets, the HCI community can foster more incisive examinations of LMs' generative capabilities.
F19.claim: the paper's argument: curating and analysing large interaction datasets lets HCI examine LM capabilities more incisively
F19.lineage: the problem: capabilities context-dependent and subjectively interpreted

F20.quote: we present CoAuthor, a dataset designed for revealing GPT-3's capabilities in assisting creative and argumentative writing.
F20.claim: the paper's definition: a dataset designed for revealing GPT-3's capabilities in assisting creative and argumentative writing
F20.lineage: what it is: a human-AI collaborative writing dataset of 1445 sessions

F21.quote: CoAuthor captures rich interactions between 63 writers and four instances of GPT-3 across 1445 writing sessions.
F21.claim: the dataset captures interactions between 63 writers and four instances of GPT-3 across 1445 writing sessions
F21.lineage: what it is: a human-AI collaborative writing dataset of 1445 sessions

F22.quote: We demonstrate that CoAuthor can address questions about GPT-3's language, ideation, and collaboration capabilities, and reveal its contribution as a writing "collaborator" under various definitions of good collaboration.
F22.claim: the paper's headline claim: the dataset can address GPT-3's language, ideation and collaboration capabilities and reveal its contribution as a writing 'collaborator' under several definitions of good collaboration
F22.lineage: the model as 'collaborator' under definitions of collaboration

F23.quote: Finally, we discuss how this work may facilitate a more principled discussion around LMs' promises and pitfalls in relation to interaction design.
F23.claim: the paper discusses how the work may make discussion of LMs' promises and pitfalls in interaction design more principled
F23.lineage: the problem: capabilities context-dependent and subjectively interpreted

F33.locus: overview, 'The CoAuthor Dataset and Methodology': Diverse Contexts
F33.quote: Diverse Contexts: The study included both creative writing (storytelling) and argumentative writing (evidence-based reasoning) tasks, using 20 different prompts sourced from Reddit's r/WritingPrompts and The New York Times.
F33.claim: the overview: creative and argumentative tasks on 20 prompts from r/WritingPrompts and The New York Times

F34.quote: Process-Oriented Data Collection: Rather than simply collecting final outputs, CoAuthor records every interaction as timestamped events, including text insertions, deletions, cursor movements, and AI suggestion requests.
F34.claim: the overview: the dataset records every interaction as timestamped events in place of final outputs alone

F35.quote: Systematic Variation: The researchers used GPT-3's davinci engine with two different randomness settings - high randomness (temperature=0.75, frequency penalty=1) and low randomness (temperature=0.3, frequency penalty=0) - to understand how model behavior affects collaboration.
F35.claim: the overview: GPT-3's davinci engine at two randomness settings, high (temperature 0.75, frequency penalty 1) and low (0.3, 0)
F35.lineage: the model instances: davinci at two randomness settings

F36.quote: The data collection involved 63 qualified crowd workers who completed 1,445 writing sessions using a custom web-based text editor. Writers could request up to five AI suggestions at any point by pressing the tab key, then choose to accept or dismiss each suggestion.
F36.claim: the overview: 63 qualified crowd workers completed 1,445 sessions in a custom web-based editor, requesting up to five suggestions with the tab key
F36.lineage: the writers: crowd workers, held under identifiers

F37.quote: Sentences generated by GPT-3 and accepted by human writers contained fewer spelling and grammatical errors (0.033 errors per word) compared to human-only text (0.037 errors per word). Notably, text segments created jointly by humans and AI showed the lowest error rates (0.032 errors per word)
F37.claim: the overview: accepted GPT-3 sentences had fewer errors per word (0.033) than human-only text (0.037), and jointly made segments the fewest (0.032)

F38.quote: The analysis showed that 13% of accepted suggestions in creative writing and 7% in argumentative writing contained new named entities (characters, locations, concepts) not present in the preceding text. … Crucially, writers subsequently reused 20% of AI-introduced named entities in creative writing and 14% in argumentative writing.
F38.claim: the overview: 13% (creative) and 7% (argumentative) of accepted suggestions introduced new named entities, and writers reused 20% and 14% of them

F39.quote: The research revealed that collaboration patterns vary significantly across individual writers but remain relatively consistent across different writing prompts.
F39.claim: the overview: collaboration patterns vary across writers and stay consistent across prompts

F40.quote: Equality: The evenness of turn-taking between human and AI … Mutuality: The level of human interaction with AI suggestions
F40.claim: the overview: the paper's two metrics, equality (evenness of turn-taking between human and AI) and mutuality (the level of human interaction with AI suggestions)
F40.lineage: collaboration measured: equality and mutuality, from ESL pair work

F41.quote: The main paper directly adapts the theoretical concepts of 'equality' and 'mutuality' from this work to create novel metrics for analyzing the collaborative dynamics between writers and GPT-3. … Neomy Storch. 2002. Patterns of interaction in ESL pair work.
F41.claim: the overview: the paper adapts equality and mutuality from Storch's study of ESL pair work (2002)
F41.lineage: collaboration measured: equality and mutuality, from ESL pair work

F42.quote: Ownership and Satisfaction: Writers reported stronger feelings of ownership when they authored a larger proportion of the final text (r=0.3). Interestingly, the amount of editing performed showed no meaningful correlation with ownership, suggesting that text origin matters more than editorial effort in human-AI collaboration.
F42.claim: the overview: writers reported stronger ownership when they authored a larger share of the final text (r=0.3); editing showed no meaningful correlation with ownership, which the overview reads as text origin mattering more than editorial effort
F42.lineage: ownership: the writer's share and the writer's sense of the text

F43.quote: Productivity Enhancement: The research found strong correlations between final text length and both the number of AI queries (r=0.42) and accepted suggestions (r=0.48).
F43.claim: the overview: final text length correlates with the number of queries (r=0.42) and accepted suggestions (r=0.48)

F44.quote: Model Training: The dataset provides supervision signals for training language models specifically for interactive, collaborative settings
F44.claim: the overview: the dataset provides supervision signals for training language models for interactive, collaborative settings

F45.lineage: reception: a paper page and its generated overview
